beginner: Peas like loose, fertile soil that drains well, with some compost mixed in. The main thing they care about is good drainage, because peas planted in cold, soggy soil tend to rot before they sprout. If water sits on your bed for a long time after rain, work in compost or plant on a raised bed first.
seasoned: Snow peas do best in a fertile, well-drained sandy loam or loam with compost worked in before sowing. The critical trait is drainage: pea seed sown into cold, wet, poorly drained ground rots before it germinates, and the soilborne root rots that follow are the main early-season risk. Steady, even moisture without waterlogging carries the crop through flowering and pod fill. Peas are legumes and fix much of their own nitrogen, so the bed needs fertility and tilth more than heavy feeding.

beginner: Peas grow best in soil from about 6.0 to 7.0, which is slightly acidic to neutral. They do poorly in strongly acidic soil below 6.0, so if a soil test reads low, mix in some lime before planting. Most garden beds are already in a good range.
seasoned: Aim for a soil pH of about 6.0 to 7.0. Clemson recommends a 6.0 to 6.5 target, and growth is inhibited on acid soils at pH 6.0 and below, so lime an acid plot the season before sowing. Peas tolerate up to roughly 7.5, and a soil test is the reliable way to confirm both pH and fertility before the season starts.

beginner: Peas make much of their own food from the air, so they barely need fertilizer. Mix a little compost or balanced fertilizer into the bed before you plant and that is enough. Too much fertilizer gives you big leafy vines but fewer pods. If you like, you can coat the seed with a pea inoculant powder, which helps the roots make nitrogen, but it is optional.
seasoned: Snow peas are light feeders. As legumes they fix much of their own nitrogen through root nodules, so heavy nitrogen drives leafy vine growth at the expense of pods. Without a soil test, work a little balanced fertilizer or compost into the bed before sowing; that is usually all peas need. An inoculant of the right Rhizobium bacteria is optional and can help nodulation where peas have not been grown before. Avoid high-nitrogen feeds, which delay flowering and cut pod set.

beginner: A balanced vegetable fertilizer like 5-10-10 mixed into the bed before planting is plenty.
seasoned: A balanced 5-10-10 worked in before sowing if no soil test is available; skip extra nitrogen, which peas supply themselves.

beginner: About 3 pounds of 5-10-10 per 100 square feet, mixed into the bed before planting.
seasoned: 5-10-10 at about 3 pounds per 100 square feet worked in before sowing, per Clemson, when no soil test is available.

beginner: Peas get along with most cool-season vegetables. They grow happily beside carrots, radishes, and lettuce, and because they leave nitrogen in the soil, they are a good crop to grow before a leafy green. The pairing to avoid is planting peas right next to onions or garlic.
seasoned: As a nitrogen-fixing legume, peas leave the soil richer for what follows and sit comfortably among the other cool-season crops grown in the same early-spring and fall windows: carrots, radishes, and lettuce are classic bed-mates. The long-standing caution is to keep peas away from the alliums (onion, garlic), which are widely held to suppress legumes through the same root-bacteria interference seen with beans.

beginner: A classic cool-season neighbor that shares peas' early-spring and fall timing; the carrots root deep while the peas climb, so they use the bed without crowding.
seasoned: Carrots and peas grow in the same cool windows and use the bed in complementary ways: the carrot works the soil deep while the pea climbs above it, and the peas' nitrogen fixation lightly benefits the carrot. The pairing is traditional and compatibility-based rather than a measured pest defense, so expect easy cohabitation more than active protection.

beginner: Radishes sprout fast and mark the pea rows while the slower peas come up, then are pulled long before the peas need the space.
seasoned: Radishes germinate in days and mark the rows while the peas emerge, and they finish and come out weeks before the peas size up, so they never compete. Both are cool-season crops sown at the same time, which makes them a tidy, low-risk interplant rather than a measured protective pairing.

beginner: Lettuce shares peas' cool-season timing and stays low, tucking in along the base of the pea row or trellis.
seasoned: Lettuce slots in below a pea trellis or alongside a bush row, sharing the same cool-season window and water needs while occupying a different layer of the bed. As the peas leaf out they offer the lettuce a little light afternoon shade that delays bolting. It is a compatibility pairing on sound shared-conditions grounds rather than a measured protective one.

beginner: Onions and other alliums are traditionally kept away from peas, which are said to grow poorly near them.
seasoned: Onions next to peas is the better-grounded of the 'bad' pairings. Alliums release antibacterial sulfur compounds that are widely held to interfere with the Rhizobium bacteria on pea roots, the bacteria the plant relies on to fix nitrogen, so pea growth tends to stall near onions. Keep them in separate parts of the bed. The useful corollary is that peas grown before an allium crop leave the soil better for it.

beginner: Like onions, garlic is a traditional bad neighbor for peas.
seasoned: Garlic acts on peas the way onions do. As an allium it gives off antibacterial sulfur compounds held to disrupt the nitrogen-fixing bacteria on pea roots, slowing the vines. Treat garlic and peas as bed-mates to keep apart, and use the pea-then-allium rotation to your advantage instead.

beginner: Clusters of small, soft green insects packed onto the growing tips, flower stems, and undersides of the leaves. They curl and yellow the new growth and stunt the plants, and they leave a sticky residue. The bigger problem is that pea aphids spread virus diseases from plant to plant, so they are worth catching early.
seasoned: Colonies of soft, pinhead-sized green aphids clustered on the growing tips, flower stalks, and leaf undersides. Heavy feeding curls and yellows the new growth, stunts the vines, and can drop blossoms; a sticky honeydew and sooty mold may follow. Most important, pea aphids transmit the virus diseases of peas, including pea enation mosaic, so even modest numbers matter.

beginner: The pea aphid, a large green aphid that multiplies quickly in the cool weather of spring and fall when peas are growing. It builds up fast, before helpful insects like ladybugs catch up.
seasoned: The pea aphid (Acyrthosiphon pisum), a large green aphid that builds up fast in the cool, mild weather of spring and fall, exactly the seasons peas grow. It reproduces rapidly, so colonies form before natural enemies catch up.

beginner: Blast the colonies off with a strong spray of water, or use insecticidal soap, which works on contact. Start as soon as you see them, while there are only a few. Ladybugs and other helpful insects usually finish the job. Since aphids spread viruses, it is worth dealing with them early.
seasoned: Knock colonies off with a strong spray of water, or treat with insecticidal soap, which controls aphids on contact; begin as soon as colonies are found, while numbers are low. Ladybugs, lacewings, and parasitic wasps usually bring populations down on their own. Because the real risk is virus transmission, act early rather than waiting for visible damage.

beginner: Lay down reflective mulch, which confuses aphids and cuts the viruses they spread, and pull nearby weeds that shelter them. Do not overfeed with fertilizer, since the soft new growth is exactly what aphids like. Where pea viruses are common, plant a resistant variety like Oregon Sugar Pod II.
seasoned: Lay reflective mulch, which disorients aphids and reduces both feeding and virus spread, and control nearby weeds and clover that harbor them. Avoid overfeeding with nitrogen, which produces the soft, lush growth aphids favor, and choose virus-resistant varieties such as Oregon Sugar Pod II where pea viruses are a known problem.

beginner: Little notches chewed out of the leaf edges of young plants, and beetles on the flowers in spring. The hidden damage is worse: the grubs tunnel into the peas forming inside the pods, leaving tiny round holes in the dried seeds. Holes in saved seed are the tell. The pea weevil eats only peas.
seasoned: Small notches chewed from the leaf margins of young plants in spring, and adults feeding on the blossoms. The real damage is hidden: larvae bore into the developing seeds inside the pods and feed there, leaving tiny round exit holes in the dried peas. Saved seed with holes is the giveaway. The pea weevil feeds only on peas (Pisum).

beginner: The pea weevil, a small brown beetle that feeds only on peas. The adults spend the winter in garden trash, move in when the peas flower to lay eggs on the young pods, and the grubs grow up inside the seeds. There is one generation each year.
seasoned: The pea weevil (Bruchus pisorum), a small brownish beetle whose host range is peas alone. Adults overwinter in debris and trash, move into the crop at bloom to lay eggs on young pods, and the larvae develop inside the seeds. There is one generation a year.

beginner: Watch for the beetles while the peas are flowering, which is when they lay eggs. Picking them off and covering the plants with a light row cover at flowering both help. At the end of the season, check dried peas for tiny round holes before you save seed, and freezing saved seed for a few days kills any grubs inside.
seasoned: Monitor for adults during bloom, when egg-laying begins. In a home patch, handpicking and floating row cover over the crop at flowering reduce egg-laying. At season's end, inspect dried peas for the small round exit holes before storing seed; freezing saved seed for several days kills any larvae inside.

beginner: Clear away and destroy the old pea plants after harvest so the beetles have nowhere to overwinter, and move your peas to a new spot each year. Do not save seed that has holes in it. Planting early so the pods finish before the beetles get busy also helps.
seasoned: Clean up and destroy pea debris after harvest to remove overwintering shelter, and rotate peas away from last year's bed. Do not save or replant seed showing exit holes. Where the weevil is established, an early sowing that finishes pod fill before peak adult activity escapes the worst.

beginner: Cutworms cut off young pea seedlings right at the soil line overnight, so you find plants toppled over and gaps in the row. Armyworms are smooth caterpillars that chew the leaves and sometimes the pods, and they can show up in numbers. Both feed at night and hide during the day.
seasoned: Cutworms sever young seedlings at or just below the soil line overnight, leaving toppled plants and thinned rows in spring. Armyworms are smooth caterpillars that chew foliage and can move through a planting in numbers, skeletonizing leaves and nicking pods. Both feed mostly at night and hide in the soil or debris by day.

beginner: Several kinds of night-feeding caterpillars: cutworms and armyworms, the young of different moths. They come in from weedy or grassy areas, and young seedlings are the most at risk.
seasoned: Several night-feeding caterpillars, including cutworms (the larvae of various moths) and beet or western yellowstriped armyworms. They overwinter or move in from weedy ground and grassy cover, and seedlings are the most vulnerable stage.

beginner: Pick the caterpillars off in the evening or early morning, and dig a little around fallen seedlings to find the curled-up cutworm. A collar of cardboard or foil around a seedling blocks cutworms, and a Bt spray controls young armyworms on the leaves. A light row cover keeps the moths from laying eggs.
seasoned: Handpick caterpillars in the evening or early morning, and check the soil around toppled seedlings for the curled cutworm. A cardboard or foil collar around a seedling stops cutworms; Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) controls young armyworms on the foliage. A floating row cover keeps egg-laying moths off the planting.

beginner: Clear weeds and tall grass before planting so the moths have fewer places to lay eggs, and turn the soil a couple of weeks before sowing to expose the grubs. Keep the edges of the bed weeded, and cover young seedlings with a row cover if these caterpillars are a problem where you are.
seasoned: Clear weeds and grassy cover before sowing to remove egg-laying sites, and turn the bed a couple of weeks ahead of planting to expose and dry out resident larvae. Keep row edges weed-free through the season, and protect emerging seedlings, the vulnerable stage, with a row cover where these caterpillars are a known problem.

beginner: Fine silvery streaks and pale flecks on the leaves and pods, with tiny dark specks, where the slender insects scrape the surface and feed. Bad infestations twist the new growth and leave scars on the pods. Thrips can also spread some viruses.
seasoned: Fine silvery or whitish scarring and flecking on leaves and pods, with tiny dark specks of excrement, as the slender insects rasp the surface and feed on the released sap. Heavy feeding distorts new growth and can scar pods cosmetically. Thrips also vector some plant viruses.

beginner: Thrips, slender insects much smaller than an aphid that build up in warm, dry weather toward the end of the pea season. They scrape the surface of the plant and feed on the sap.
seasoned: Several thrips species, slender insects a fraction the size of an aphid that build up in warm, dry stretches late in the pea season. They rasp the plant surface and feed on the sap that wells up.

beginner: Peas usually shrug off a little thrips damage. If they build up, a strong spray of water and insecticidal soap knock them back, and helpful insects pitch in. Keep the plants watered and unstressed, since dried-out peas are more likely to be hit.
seasoned: Peas usually outgrow light thrips feeding without treatment. Where numbers climb, a strong spray of water and insecticidal soap reduce them, and natural enemies such as minute pirate bugs and lacewings help. Keep plants unstressed and well watered, since drought-stressed peas are more prone.

beginner: Pull nearby weeds that shelter thrips, lay reflective mulch to confuse them, and keep the soil evenly moist so the plants are not stressed. Most home pea crops are done before thrips become a real problem.
seasoned: Control weeds that harbor thrips, lay reflective mulch to disorient them and reduce virus spread, and keep moisture even so plants are not drought-stressed. Most home pea crops finish before thrips become a real problem.

beginner: A white to gray powdery dust that starts as spots on top of the leaves and spreads over the leaves, stems, and pods. The leaves yellow and dry out, the vines weaken, and the pods can be spotted. It is the classic late-season pea problem, showing up as the weather warms and dries toward the end of the spring crop.
seasoned: A white to grayish powdery coating that starts as small spots on the upper leaf surfaces and spreads to cover leaves, stems, and pods. Affected leaves yellow and dry, vines lose vigor, and pods may be spotted or off-flavored. It is the classic late-season pea disease, arriving as the spring crop runs into warmer, drier weather.

beginner: A fungus (Erysiphe pisi) that thrives in warm days, cool nights, and dry leaves, which is exactly the weather at the end of the pea season. It spreads on the wind and moves fast once it starts, so catching it early and planting resistant varieties matter most.
seasoned: The fungus Erysiphe pisi, favored by warm days, cool nights, and dry foliage, the conditions that arrive late in the pea season. Spores spread on the wind, and the disease moves fast once established, which is why early control and resistant varieties matter most.

beginner: Powdery mildew is easiest to handle the moment you first see it; once it covers the leaves, it is hard to stop. Pick off the worst leaves and open up the planting for airflow. A sulfur spray started early and repeated per the label helps. If the spring crop is nearly finished, the simplest move is to pick what is ready and pull the plants.
seasoned: Powdery mildew is best managed at the very first signs; once it covers the leaves and yellowing sets in, control is difficult. Remove the worst-affected leaves and improve airflow. Sulfur or a labeled biofungicide, begun early and repeated per the label, suppresses it. On a spring crop that is nearly done, harvesting promptly and pulling the planting is often the practical choice.

beginner: Plant a resistant variety, which is the best defense: Oregon Sugar Pod II and many newer snow peas resist powdery mildew. Plant early so the crop finishes before the mildew weather arrives, give the plants room and a trellis so air moves through them, and stay out of the patch when the vines are wet.
seasoned: Choose resistant varieties, the single most effective step: Oregon Sugar Pod II and many modern snow peas carry powdery mildew resistance. Sow early so the crop finishes pod fill before the late-season mildew weather, give plants room and a trellis for airflow, and avoid working among wet vines.

beginner: The lower leaves turn yellow and the yellowing creeps up the plant, which becomes stunted, curls, and wilts. If you cut the lower stem, the tissue inside is stained reddish or orange. Affected plants often die before making a crop. It shows up in patches and gets worse as the soil warms.
seasoned: A yellowing of the lower leaves that progresses up the plant, with downward curling, stunting, and wilting; a cut through the lower stem shows a reddish or orange discoloration of the water-conducting tissue. Plants often die before pod fill. Symptoms appear in patches and worsen as the soil warms.

beginner: A fungus that lives in the soil and enters through the roots, clogging the plant's plumbing. It survives in the soil for years and likes warm soil. Once it is in a bed you cannot get rid of it, so the answer is resistant varieties and moving your peas around.
seasoned: The soilborne fungus Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. pisi, which enters through the roots, plugs the vascular system, and persists in the soil for years. Several races exist. Warm soil favors it, and once a bed is infested the fungus cannot be eradicated, so resistant varieties and rotation are the management.

beginner: There is no cure once a plant is infected; pull and throw away (do not compost) the affected plants. You manage this one by preventing it, with resistant varieties and rotation, not by spraying.
seasoned: There is no cure for infected plants; remove and destroy them to limit buildup. Management is preventive: the disease is handled through resistant varieties and rotation, not treatment.

beginner: Plant a wilt-resistant variety, which most modern snow peas are (Oregon Sugar Pod II, Dwarf Gray Sugar, Mammoth Melting Sugar all resist it). Move your peas to a new spot on a three-to-four-year cycle, improve drainage, and avoid carrying infected soil from bed to bed.
seasoned: Plant Fusarium-resistant varieties, which are widely available (Oregon Sugar Pod II, Dwarf Gray Sugar, and Mammoth Melting Sugar all carry wilt resistance). Rotate peas on a three-to-four-year cycle away from infested ground, improve drainage, and avoid moving infested soil between beds.

beginner: Seeds that rot before they come up, and seedlings that flop over at a pinched, water-soaked spot near the soil. On bigger plants the roots rot, the vines stunt, and the lower leaves yellow and die. It is worst in cold, wet, poorly drained soil that makes the seed sit too long before sprouting.
seasoned: Seed that rots before emerging, and seedlings that damp off, collapsing at a water-soaked, pinched stem base. On older plants the root rot complex stunts the vines, yellows and kills the lower leaves, and rots the roots and lower stem brown. Damage is worst in cold, wet, poorly drained soil that slows germination and keeps seedlings vulnerable.

beginner: A group of soil fungi and water molds (including Pythium, Rhizoctonia, and Aphanomyces) that attack seeds, roots, and seedlings. Cold, soggy soil and damaged roots at planting let them in, and they build up where peas are grown too often in the same spot.
seasoned: A complex of soilborne fungi and water molds, chiefly Pythium, Rhizoctonia, Fusarium solani, and Aphanomyces euteiches. Cold, saturated soil and root injury at planting set the stage; Aphanomyces in particular builds up in beds cropped to peas too often and severe infections kill plants outright.

beginner: There is no saving seed or seedlings that have rotted; replant once the soil is warmer and drains better. Pulling affected plants and improving drainage help, but the main thing is preventing it, since these organisms live in the soil.
seasoned: There is no rescue for rotted seed or collapsed seedlings; replant into warmer, better-drained conditions once the soil has dried. Removing affected plants and improving drainage limits further loss, but prevention is the real lever since the organisms are already in the soil.

beginner: Plant in well-drained soil or raised beds instead of cold, wet, low spots, and never sow peas into soggy ground. Avoid damaging the roots when planting, move your peas around the garden on a three-to-four-year cycle, and clear away the old plants after harvest.
seasoned: Sow into well-drained ground or raised beds rather than cold, low, wet spots, and do not sow peas into waterlogged soil. Avoid root injury at planting, rotate peas on a three-to-four-year cycle to keep Aphanomyces down, and clear crop debris after harvest. Some varieties offer partial root-rot tolerance.

beginner: Brown to purple-black spots and streaks on the leaves, stems, and pods, sometimes with a blackened stem base. Sunken spots on the pods can carry the disease into the seed. It shows up in cool, wet spring and fall weather and rides in on infected seed and old plant debris.
seasoned: Brown to purplish-black spots and streaks on leaves, stems, and pods, often with darker margins; a blackening at the base of the stem (foot rot) in one form, and sunken lesions on the pods that can carry the fungus into the seed. It develops in cool, wet spring and fall weather and is carried on infected seed and debris.

beginner: A group of related fungi that survive on infected seed and on old pea plants left in the soil. Cool, wet weather and splashing water spread them. Once they are on the seed, they travel with it to the next planting.
seasoned: A complex of related fungi (the Ascochyta blight complex, including Ascochyta pisi and Mycosphaerella pinodes). The fungi survive on infected seed and on pea debris in the soil, and cool, wet conditions with splashing water drive infection and spread.

beginner: You cannot cure tissue that is already infected; pull and throw away (do not compost) affected plants and all the old debris to slow it down. For a home garden, prevention does most of the work, since the disease travels on seed and old plants.
seasoned: There is no cure for infected tissue; remove and destroy affected plants and all debris to limit spread. Cultural control is the mainstay for a home crop, since the disease is seed- and debris-borne.

beginner: Plant certified disease-free seed and do not save seed from an infected crop. Clear away all the old pea plants after harvest, and do not grow peas in that spot for at least three to four years. Water at the base, not overhead, and stay out of the patch when the vines are wet.
seasoned: Plant certified disease-free seed and do not save seed from an infected crop. Remove all pea debris after harvest and rotate peas off the ground for a minimum of three to four years before returning. Avoid overhead watering and working among wet vines, which splash and carry the fungus.

beginner: Water regularly so the soil stays evenly moist but not soggy. Pay closest attention while the plants are flowering and the pods are filling out.
seasoned: Regular and even through the season, keeping the soil moist but never waterlogged. The need peaks during flowering and pod fill; before that, established vines in cool weather ask relatively little.

beginner: Water deeply enough to wet the soil about 6 inches down. Deep, less frequent watering beats a daily light sprinkle.
seasoned: Enough to wet the root zone roughly 6 inches down; watering deeply and less often builds deeper roots than frequent light sprinkles. Clemson advises watering to moisten the soil to a depth of 6 inches.

beginner: Water the soil, not the leaves, and do it in the morning so the plants dry off during the day. Wet leaves, especially overnight, help spread disease.
seasoned: Water at the soil level in the morning so the foliage dries before evening; this limits the powdery mildew and Ascochyta the crop is prone to. Avoid overhead watering on a trellised crop in particular.

beginner: If the soil is wet but the plants still wilt or the lower leaves turn yellow, you may be overwatering. Soggy soil rots pea roots.
seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves, wilting despite wet soil, and stunted vines point to waterlogged roots and the onset of the root rots peas are prone to in cold, wet ground.

beginner: If plants dry out while flowering, they drop their flowers and the pods come out small and tough. Keep the water steady at that stage.
seasoned: Drought stress during and after flowering aborts blossoms and produces small, tough, stringy pods, and it hastens the late-season decline as heat arrives.

beginner: Keep the soil evenly damp, not soggy, until the seedlings come up. Pea seeds rot in cold, wet ground.
seasoned: Direct-sown into cool soil, snow peas want an evenly moist seedbed until emergence, but not soggy: pea seed rots in cold, waterlogged ground.

beginner: Keep the young plants evenly watered as they get going and start to climb.
seasoned: Grow the young vines on with steady, even moisture as they root out and start to climb.

beginner: In cool weather the growing vines need fairly little water. Soak the soil about 6 inches down, in the morning at the soil so the leaves dry off. Do not overwater peas before they flower.
seasoned: Established vines in cool weather ask relatively little: water deeply enough to wet the root zone about 6 inches down (Clemson advises moistening to 6 inches), at soil level in the morning so foliage dries and powdery mildew and Ascochyta stay down. Do not overwater a cool-season crop before it flowers.

beginner: Keep the water steady once the peas flower. Drought now drops the blossoms and you get fewer pods.
seasoned: Flowering is moisture-critical: stress here aborts blossoms and directly cuts the crop. Keep the soil evenly moist and water at the base, avoiding overhead wetting on the trellised vines.

beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist while the pods fill. Snow peas turn small, tough, and stringy if they dry out now, so steady water gives you tender, flat pods.
seasoned: Pod fill is the peak: stress here toughens the flat edible pods and leaves them small and stringy. Keep moisture steady right through filling.

beginner: Keep watering evenly while you pick the flat pods. Steady water keeps them tender, though the vines naturally fade as the weather warms up.
seasoned: Keep even moisture through the picking run; steady water holds pod quality, though the crop naturally winds down as heat arrives and hastens the late-season decline.

beginner: Try not to spray the whole plant from above. The most important time to keep water steady is when the plants are flowering and forming pods.
seasoned: Avoid overhead watering where practical; the critical moisture window is flowering through pod fill.

beginner: Flowering and pod-filling are the times peas most need steady water.
seasoned: Flowering and pod fill are the moisture-critical stages; stress here directly cuts the crop and toughens the pods.

beginner: You do not need to harden off peas. They are planted straight into the garden from seed.
seasoned: Not applicable. Peas are direct-sown in place and are not started indoors or hardened off.

beginner: Plant pea seeds right where they will grow, as soon as the soil can be worked in spring and again in late summer for fall. Peas do not like their roots disturbed, so skip starting them indoors. Plant about 1 to 1.5 inches deep.
seasoned: Direct-sow into cool, workable soil as early as the ground can be prepared in spring, and again for a fall crop. Peas resent root disturbance and germinate readily in cool soil, so transplanting offers no advantage. Sow about 1 to 1.5 inches deep; some growers presoak seed overnight to speed emergence.

beginner: Use a good potting mix, not garden soil, which packs down too hard in pots.
seasoned: A well-draining potting mix; avoid native garden soil, which compacts and drains poorly in containers and worsens root rot.

beginner: Mix in a little compost for fertility.
seasoned: Blend in compost for baseline fertility and tilth; peas need little added nitrogen.

beginner: Pots dry out faster than garden beds, so check the soil daily in warm weather and water when the top inch is dry.
seasoned: Containers dry faster than beds; monitor daily in warm spells and water when the top inch dries.

beginner: Container peas still need little feeding; a little compost in the mix is usually enough.
seasoned: Feeding needs stay low in containers; compost blended into the mix usually suffices.

beginner: Not applicable. Peas are a cool-season annual; they finish in one season and are not overwintered as a plant.
seasoned: Not applicable. As a single-season annual, peas complete their cycle and are pulled; in mild regions a fall sowing is grown over winter in the ground, but a container crop is grown and finished within a season.

beginner: Bush and dwarf snow peas grow well in a pot at least 5 gallons and 8 inches deep. Push a few short twiggy branches or a small trellis into the pot for the tendrils to climb, plant several seeds, and keep the mix evenly moist.
seasoned: Dwarf and bush snow pea types suit containers well; tall climbing varieties are awkward in pots because of their trellis height. A pot of at least 5 gallons and 8 inches deep, planted with several seeds and given a few twiggy branches or a small trellis for support, performs well with even moisture.

beginner: A self-watering pot is a good match for peas because it keeps the water steady, which is what they like, without leaving the roots soggy.
seasoned: A self-watering container suits peas well, smoothing out the steady moisture they want through pod fill while avoiding the soggy roots they dislike.

beginner: Pick the pot to fit the variety. Low bush peas do well in a wide pot with several plants together; tall climbing peas need a deep, heavy pot that will not tip over once the trellis is loaded with vines. For a pot, a short bush variety is usually the easier pick.
seasoned: Match the container to the variety: a wide, shallow pot suits low bush types grown several together, while a tall climbing variety needs a deep, stable pot that will not tip under a loaded trellis. For most container growers a dwarf or bush snow pea in a broad pot is the easier choice.

beginner: Do not plant peas where peas or beans grew last year. Diseases build up in the soil and hit the next crop. If you have had root rot or blight, wait even longer, up to four years, before peas return.
seasoned: Avoid following peas with peas or other legumes in the same bed; rotate to break the soilborne disease cycle (root rots, Fusarium, Ascochyta) that peas are prone to. Where Ascochyta or Aphanomyces root rot have appeared, extend the rotation toward four years.

beginner: Move your peas to a new spot each year, on about a three-year rotation, and longer if you have had disease trouble. Because peas feed the soil with nitrogen, whatever you plant there next will benefit.
seasoned: Rotate peas on a roughly three-year cycle, longer where Ascochyta blight or root rot have shown up. Their nitrogen-fixing habit makes them a good predecessor for nitrogen-hungry crops.

beginner: Do not leave snow peas out on the counter. They go limp and lose their sweetness quickly, so cool them soon after picking.
seasoned: Not recommended. Snow peas lose sweetness and crispness fast at room temperature and should be cooled promptly after picking rather than held on the counter.

beginner: Cool the pods right after picking, then keep them in the fridge in a loosely closed bag. They stay good for about five days when kept cold and slightly damp; the longer they sit, the less sweet they get.
seasoned: Cool snow peas immediately after harvest to shed field heat, then refrigerate in a perforated bag. They hold good quality for about five days kept cold and humid, near 32 to 40°F at high humidity; the sugars convert to starch over time, so use them sooner rather than later.

beginner: Snow peas freeze well for keeping longer. Give them a quick dip in boiling water (blanch), cool them, and freeze within a few hours of picking for the best result.
seasoned: Snow peas freeze well for longer storage. Blanch briefly to set the color and texture, cool, and freeze within a few hours of picking for the best quality.

beginner: Snow peas taste best soon after picking. To keep them, cool them fast, store them cold and slightly damp, and freeze (after a quick blanch) within a few hours if you want them to last beyond a few days.
seasoned: Snow peas are at their sweetest within hours of picking and are best used promptly. To hold them, cool them fast to remove field heat, keep them cold and humid, and blanch and freeze within a few hours if you want to store them beyond a few days.

beginner: These are snow peas, the flat kind you eat pod and all while the pods are still flat and the peas inside are tiny. They are different from sugar snap peas, which are plump and rounded and eaten when filled out. Oregon Sugar Pod II and Dwarf Gray Sugar are easy, dependable choices; pick a short bush type if you do not want to build a tall trellis.
seasoned: These are flat-podded snow (mangetout) peas, picked young while the pods are flat and the seeds barely formed. Do not confuse them with sugar snap peas, a separate edible-pod type bred for plump, rounded pods eaten whole once filled. Lean to powdery-mildew- and wilt-resistant varieties such as Oregon Sugar Pod II where those diseases recur, and match the variety's height to your support: bush types stand alone, tall types need a trellis.

beginner: Bare soil for a week or so, then the little plants push up. Peas come up in cool soil and can go in very early, but seed planted in cold, soggy ground rots instead of sprouting. They come up fastest when the soil is around 55 to 65°F.
seasoned: Bare soil for about a week to ten days, then the seedling pushes up through the surface. Peas germinate in cool soil and can be sown as soon as the ground is workable, but seed sown into cold, saturated ground rots before it emerges. Emergence is quickest in soil around 55 to 65°F and slows below that; the lower limit for germination is about 40°F.

beginner: Plant as soon as you can work the soil, about 1 to 1.5 inches deep, in moist but well-drained ground. Do not keep the bed soggy after planting, since that rots the seed. Soaking the seeds overnight before planting can speed things up.
seasoned: Sow as early as the soil can be worked, about 1 to 1.5 inches deep, into a moist but well-drained bed; do not sow into waterlogged ground. There is no benefit to soaking the bed afterward, which suffocates the seed and feeds root rot. An optional overnight presoak of the seed speeds emergence, and a pea inoculant helps nodulation where peas are new to the bed.

beginner: Have your peas come up yet? Write down the date you first saw them break the soil.
seasoned: Have your peas emerged? Note the date to track days to maturity from a real sowing rather than the seed packet.

beginner: Small plants a few inches tall with their first leaves and the little curling tendrils that peas use to climb. Young peas handle light frost fine, but this is when cutworms can cut them off at the ground and slugs can chew them in wet weather.
seasoned: Young plants a few inches tall putting out their first leaves and, soon, the curling tendrils that mark a climbing crop. Pea seedlings are cold-hardy and shrug off light spring frost, but they are the stage most vulnerable to cutworms, which sever them at the soil line, and to slugs in wet weather.

beginner: Put up the support now, before the vines sprawl: a trellis, netting, or twiggy branches alongside the row, even for short types. Keep the soil evenly moist, pull weeds early, and weed shallowly so you do not damage the roots. Check for plants cut off at the ground, which means cutworms.
seasoned: Set up support now, before the vines flop: push twiggy branches or a trellis or netting in alongside even bush types, which crop better held up. Keep the bed evenly moist and weed-free, cultivate shallowly since pea roots run near the surface, and watch for toppled seedlings that signal cutworms.

beginner: How do your young pea plants look? Note any chewed or toppled plants and whether the tendrils are reaching for the trellis.
seasoned: How is your pea stand looking? Note any gaps, cutworm damage, or the first tendrils reaching for support.

beginner: The vines climb and fill in, their tendrils grabbing the support as they go. Short types reach two to three feet, tall types four to five. Peas make much of their own food (nitrogen) at this stage, so you want healthy green growth, not huge dark leafy vines, which usually mean too much fertilizer and fewer pods.
seasoned: Steady growth as the vines climb and fill the trellis, tendrils gripping as they go. Bush types reach two to three feet and stand together; tall types climb to four or five feet. The plants are fixing much of their own nitrogen now through root nodules, so vigorous green growth, not dark, overfed lushness, is the goal.

beginner: Keep the watering steady and do not add fertilizer now. Peas need very little, and extra just gives you big leafy vines with fewer pods. Help the first tendrils find the trellis, and keep the plants from getting crowded so air moves through them.
seasoned: Keep moisture steady and resist the urge to feed; peas need little nitrogen and extra now pushes foliage at the expense of pods. Guide the first tendrils onto the support, and keep the rows open for airflow to hold off powdery mildew as the weather warms.

beginner: How tall are your pea vines getting? Note how well they are climbing the trellis.
seasoned: How are your pea vines filling in? Note their height and whether they are climbing the support cleanly.

beginner: Small white (sometimes pink or purple) flowers open along the vines. This is an important time for water: if the plants dry out or it stays hotter than about 80°F, the flowers drop without making pods. The flowers and tiny pods are much more sensitive to frost than the young plants were.
seasoned: Small white (sometimes pink or purple) pea flowers open along the vines. This is a moisture-critical stage: water stress now aborts blossoms, and sustained heat above about 80°F causes the plant to drop flowers instead of setting pods. The flowers and tiny pods are far more frost-tender than the hardy seedlings were.

beginner: Keep the water steady and generous while the plants flower, because dry soil now means fewer peas. Water the soil, not the leaves. Cover the plants overnight if a frost threatens the open flowers, and water deeply before a heat wave. The plants set pods again once it cools, but the spring crop is running out of cool weather by now.
seasoned: Keep moisture steady and ample through bloom; this is where water stress directly cuts the crop. Avoid overhead watering on the dense canopy. If a late frost threatens open flowers, cover the planting overnight, and in a heat wave water deeply ahead of time; the plant will set again when it cools, but the spring crop is racing the heat at this point.

beginner: Are your peas flowering yet? Note when the flowers opened and whether any dropped in hot weather.
seasoned: Are your peas flowering? Note the date bloom started and any blossom drop in heat.

beginner: Flat pods form where the flowers were and grow quickly. With snow peas you want to pick them while they are still flat, bright green, and tender, before the little peas inside start to swell. They are ready about a week after the flowers open, and they get tough and stringy fast if you leave them.
seasoned: Flat pods form where the flowers were and lengthen quickly. For snow peas the pickable window is brief and early: harvest while the pods are still flat, bright, and tender, before the seeds inside begin to swell and round out the pod. Snow peas reach this stage about a week after flowering. Left on the vine they turn tough, fibrous, and starchy fast.

beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist while the pods grow. Start checking the vines every day once the first pods appear, because snow peas are tender for only a short time before they get tough.
seasoned: Maintain even moisture right through pod fill, the payoff stage for steady watering. Begin checking the vines daily as the first pods size up, since the snow-pea window is short and the pods go from tender to tough in a few days.

beginner: Are pods forming? Note when you first saw them and how quickly they are growing.
seasoned: Are pods forming? Note the date you first saw flat pods and how fast they are sizing up.

beginner: Flat, bright, crisp pods picked while the peas inside are still tiny, about a week after flowering. Pick every couple of days: regular picking keeps more pods coming, while pods left to fill up tell the plant to quit. Snow peas crop for a few weeks, then fade as it warms up.
seasoned: Flat, bright, crisp pods snapped from the vine while the seeds inside are still tiny, about 7 days after flowering. Picking every couple of days is essential: regular harvest keeps the vines flowering and producing, while pods left to mature signal the plant to stop. Most snow peas crop over a few weeks, then decline as the heat builds.

beginner: Pick in the cool morning, holding the vine with one hand and pulling the pod with the other so you do not tear the stem. Pick every two or three days, because old pods left on the plant make it stop producing. When the vines fade in the heat, pull them up and compost them.
seasoned: Pick in the cool of the morning, holding the vine with one hand and the pod with the other so you do not tear the brittle stems. Harvest every two to three days; leaving overmature pods on the vine ends the crop early. Pull the planting once it declines in the heat and add the vines to the compost, roots left to return their nitrogen.

beginner: Have you picked your first snow peas? Note the date and how they turned out.
seasoned: Have you made your first picking? Log the date and how the pods sized up.

beginner: Time to plant peas
seasoned: Time to sow peas

beginner: Plant snow peas as soon as you can work the soil in spring, even weeks before the last frost, since young peas handle cold. Plant about 1 to 1.5 inches deep in moist, well-drained soil, and put up a trellis when you plant.
seasoned: Direct-sow snow peas as early as the soil can be worked in spring, well before the last frost; pea seedlings are cold-hardy. Sow about 1 to 1.5 inches deep into a moist, well-drained bed, and set up support at sowing.

beginner: Plant your next row of peas
seasoned: Sow your next short row of peas

beginner: Snow peas give a crop over a few weeks, then slow down in the heat. Plant a new short row now, about two weeks after the last one, to keep peas coming. Stop early enough that the last batch finishes before it gets hot.
seasoned: Snow peas crop over a few weeks, then decline as the weather warms. Sow a fresh short row now, about two weeks after the last, to stretch the spring harvest. Stop in time for the crop to finish before summer heat sets in.

beginner: Start checking your snow peas every day
seasoned: Start checking your snow peas daily

beginner: Most snow peas are ready about 55 to 70 days from planting, about a week after they flower. Start checking every day and pick the pods while they are flat and tender, before the peas inside swell. Pick every two or three days to keep more coming.
seasoned: Most snow peas are ready about 55 to 70 days from sowing, roughly a week after flowering. Begin checking daily and pick the pods while they are flat, bright, and tender, before the seeds swell. Harvest every two to three days to keep the vines producing.

seasoned: Frost expected, protect flowering peas

beginner: Plant peas as early as you can work the soil, but make sure it drains well and is not soggy. Pea seeds sprout in cool soil but rot in cold, wet mud, which is the usual reason for gaps in the row. Good drainage matters more than planting on an exact date.
seasoned: Sow peas as soon as the soil can be worked, but into moist, well-drained ground, not cold mud. Pea seed germinates from about 40°F up and fastest at 55 to 65°F, yet it rots in cold, saturated soil, the most common cause of a thin stand. Raised beds and good drainage matter more than calendar date.

beginner: Peas make their own nitrogen with the help of tiny bacteria on their roots. If peas or beans have grown in your bed before, the bacteria are already there. In a brand-new bed you can coat the seed with a pea inoculant powder to help, but it is optional.
seasoned: Peas fix their own nitrogen with Rhizobium bacteria on their roots. Where peas or beans have grown before, those bacteria are already present; in a new bed, an inexpensive seed inoculant can improve nodulation. It is optional, not required, and no substitute for good drainage and tilth.

beginner: Put up the trellis or netting early, when you plant or right after. Even short peas do better held up off the ground, and tall ones need support before they start to flop. If you wait too long you can tear the vines or hurt the roots putting it in.
seasoned: Put the support in early, at or just after sowing. Even bush peas crop better and stay cleaner held up off the ground, and tall types must have a trellis or netting before the vines start to sprawl. Setting it up later risks tearing the brittle vines and damaging shallow roots.

beginner: Do not add nitrogen fertilizer now. Peas make much of their own from the air, and extra fertilizer just gives you big leafy vines with fewer peas. A little compost mixed into the bed before planting is all they need.
seasoned: Hold off on nitrogen. As legumes, peas fix much of their own through root nodules, and extra nitrogen now drives leafy vine growth at the expense of flowers and pods. A little compost or balanced fertilizer worked in before sowing is all peas need.

beginner: Keep the water steady and generous while the plants flower. Flowering and pod-filling are when peas most need water, and letting them dry out now means fewer peas. Water the soil in the morning, not the leaves, to keep disease down.
seasoned: Keep moisture steady and ample through bloom. Flowering and pod fill are the moisture-critical stages, and water stress now aborts blossoms and shrinks the crop. Water at the soil in the morning, not overhead, to keep the canopy dry and slow powdery mildew.

beginner: The spring crop is in a race with the heat. Once it stays above about 80°F, peas drop their flowers instead of making pods, so a planting that flowers as summer arrives makes few peas. Plant early, and where summer comes fast, pick the earliest, quickest snow peas.
seasoned: The spring crop is racing the heat. Once sustained temperatures pass about 80°F, peas drop blossoms instead of setting pods, so a planting that flowers into early summer heat sets poorly. Sow early, and where summers come on fast, lean to the earliest, shortest-season snow peas.

beginner: Pick snow peas while the pods are still flat, before the peas inside fill out. That flat, tender pod is the whole point; once the peas swell, the pod gets tough. They are ready about a week after flowering, so start checking early.
seasoned: Pick snow peas while the pods are still flat, before the seeds swell. The whole point of a snow pea is the tender flat pod; once the peas inside round out, the pod turns tough and starchy. They reach pickable size about a week after flowering, so start checking early.

beginner: Pick every two or three days. Snow peas crop for a short time, and leaving old pods on the vine tells the plant to quit. Picking often keeps more pods coming and catches them while they are flat, sweet, and tender.
seasoned: Pick every two to three days. Snow peas crop over a short window, and leaving mature pods on the vine signals the plant to stop flowering and ends the crop early. Frequent picking keeps the vines producing and catches the pods at their flat, sweet, tender best.

beginner: Each pea plant gives only a modest amount, so peas are grown in rows, not one at a time. A 10-foot row of snow peas gives about 3 to 4 pounds of pods over its picking weeks.
seasoned: Snow peas yield modestly per plant, so they are grown in rows or blocks rather than singly. Utah State puts a snow or snap pea crop at about 3 to 4 pounds of pods per 10 feet of row over its cropping window; a trellised double row in a small bed gives a steady picking for several weeks.

beginner: Snow peas crop for a few weeks, then slow down as it heats up. Most of the harvest comes in that stretch, so planting a second short row a week or two later, and a fall crop where it works, keeps peas coming longer.
seasoned: Snow peas come on over a few weeks and then decline as the weather warms. Most of a sowing's crop arrives in that window, which is why a couple of succession sowings a week or two apart, and a separate fall crop where summers allow, are the way to stretch the supply.

beginner: Snow peas are a great first-year crop. You plant the seed straight into cool spring soil, and in about two months you are picking flat, sweet pods. The main things that affect your harvest are planting early before the heat, giving the vines a trellis, and picking often while the pods are flat.
seasoned: Snow peas are a rewarding first-year crop: cold-hardy seed sown straight into early-spring soil, quick to a flat, sweet pod in about 55 to 70 days, and forgiving of cool weather. The main levers on yield are sowing early enough to beat the heat, giving the vines support, and picking often while the pods are flat.

beginner: Flowers fell off without making pods
seasoned: Flowers dropped or no pods set

beginner: The plants flowered but made few or no pods, because it got too hot. Once it stays above about 80°F, peas drop their flowers instead of making pods, and the few that form are tough. This usually happens to a spring crop planted too late that runs into summer heat. It is a weather problem, not a disease.
seasoned: The vines flowered but set few or no pods, because the weather turned too warm. Once sustained temperatures pass about 80°F, peas abort their blossoms instead of setting pods, and any pods that form are tough and stringy. It is the classic fate of a spring crop sown too late, caught by early-summer heat, and it is a weather problem, not a disease.

beginner: Plant as early as you can work the soil so the peas flower and fill in cool weather, before the heat. Where summer comes fast, pick the quickest snow peas, and try a fall planting timed to finish as it cools down.
seasoned: Sow as early as the soil can be worked so the crop flowers and fills pods in cool weather, well before summer heat. Where summers come on fast, choose the earliest short-season snow peas, and add a fall sowing timed so the crop matures in cooling weather.

beginner: Seeds rotted or did not come up
seasoned: Seed rotted or came up poorly

beginner: The seed went into cold, soggy soil and rotted instead of sprouting, or came up thin and patchy. Peas like cool soil, but wet, poorly drained ground rots the seed and lets soil fungi get to it. Planting too early into a wet bed is the usual reason for gaps.
seasoned: The seed was sown into cold, saturated soil and rotted before emerging, or came up as a thin, patchy stand. Peas tolerate cool soil, but waterlogged ground starves the seed of oxygen and feeds the soilborne root rots, so a too-early sowing into a wet, poorly drained bed is the usual cause of gaps.

beginner: Plant in well-drained soil or raised beds instead of cold, wet, low spots, and wait until the soil is workable, not muddy. Plant about 1 to 1.5 inches deep, do not keep the bed soggy, and soaking the seeds overnight helps them come up faster.
seasoned: Sow into well-drained ground or raised beds rather than cold, low, wet spots, and wait for the surface to be workable rather than muddy. Plant about 1 to 1.5 inches deep, do not keep the bed soggy, and an overnight presoak helps the seed get up and out of harm's way faster.

beginner: White powdery dust on the leaves and pods
seasoned: White powdery coating late in the crop

beginner: A white to gray powdery dust spread over the leaves and pods as the weather warmed up and the nights stayed cool. This is powdery mildew, the classic late-season pea disease. It weakens the plants and spoils the pods, and it is hard to stop once it has spread.
seasoned: A white to gray powdery film spread over the leaves, stems, and pods as the crop ran into warm days and cool nights, the conditions that favor powdery mildew. It is the classic end-of-season pea disease; it weakens the vines, taints the pods, and is hard to stop once it has covered the foliage.

beginner: Plant a resistant variety, which works best (Oregon Sugar Pod II and many newer snow peas resist mildew), and plant early so the crop finishes before mildew weather arrives. Give the vines a trellis and room to breathe, water at the soil, and pull the old plants once the spring crop is done.
seasoned: Plant powdery-mildew-resistant varieties, the most effective step (Oregon Sugar Pod II and many modern snow peas resist it), and sow early so the crop finishes before the mildew weather. Give the vines a trellis and room for airflow, water at the soil, and pull a spent spring planting promptly.

beginner: Pods came out tough and stringy
seasoned: Pods tough, stringy, or starchy

beginner: The pods came out tough and stringy instead of flat and tender, usually because they were left on the vine too long, until the peas inside swelled, or because heat and dry soil hit while the pods were filling. Snow peas need to be picked young and go from tender to tough in just a few days.
seasoned: The snow pods came out fibrous and starchy rather than flat and tender, usually because they were left on the vine past their brief pickable window, when the swelling seeds toughen the pod, or because heat and drought stress hit during pod fill. Snow peas are a pick-young crop and go from tender to tough in a few days.

beginner: Pick every two or three days while the pods are still flat, before the peas swell, starting about a week after the flowers open. Keep the water steady while the pods fill, and plant early so they grow in cool weather, not heat.
seasoned: Pick every two to three days while the pods are still flat and bright, before the seeds round out, starting about a week after flowering. Keep moisture steady through pod fill, and sow early so the pods size up in cool rather than hot weather.

beginner: Plant a little patch of snow peas every week or two instead of all at once, so you get a steady supply before the heat ends them. Do this through cool spring, and again in late summer for fall where it works. In hot areas, skip summer and keep sowing through the cool months.
seasoned: Snow peas crop over a short window and then decline in the heat, so sow small batches a week or two apart through the cool spring window rather than all at once, and again for fall where summers allow. In hot regions skip summer entirely and succession-sow through the cool fall, winter, and early spring.

beginner: In cold regions, grow snow peas in spring, and again in fall where you can. Plant as soon as you can work the soil in spring, even before the last frost, because young peas handle cold. You harvest in early summer, then the heat ends the crop. Plant again in late summer for a fall crop, since peas take the first light frosts. In the mildest cold zones a fall planting can grow through the cool months for a winter and spring harvest.
seasoned: Across the cold northern tier snow peas are a spring crop, with a second fall crop where the season allows. Sow as soon as the ground can be worked, even weeks before the last frost, since pea seedlings are cold-hardy; the spring crop is harvested in late spring to early summer and then ends as midsummer heat stops the vines and brings on powdery mildew. The hot weeks are left out, and a late-summer sowing gives a fall crop the frost-tolerant plants carry into autumn. From the milder end of the region (zone 7) a fall sowing can be grown through the cool months for a winter-into-spring harvest. The summer gap here is a true heat exclusion for peas, backed at each cell.

beginner: In the Rio Grande Valley, grow snow peas in the cool season, not summer. Plant Oct 1 through Nov 15 and harvest from Nov 30 into spring; it rarely if ever frosts here, so the challenge is heat, not cold. Snow peas are not in a TAMU RGV vegetable table by that name, so treat this window conservatively: sow direct in fall alongside the other cool-season crops for a quick winter crop of flat, edible pods. Skip planting snow peas from spring through summer: the Valley heat keeps them from growing well here.
seasoned: Snow peas in the RGV run on the winter-garden calendar: direct-sow Oct 1 through Nov 15, with harvest running Nov 30 through Jan 24. No RGV-specific table row names snow peas; this cell uses a conservative fall direct-sow window matching the general cool-season English-pea pattern, with a 60 to 70 day maturity typical of the type. Frost is essentially absent here, so timing is heat-bounded rather than cold-bounded. Windows are authored identically for zones 9 and 10: the TAMU AgriLife sources describe a single Valley-wide planting calendar, not a zone-9/zone-10 split.

beginner: West of the Cascades, snow peas love this cool, mild region. In the Willamette Valley and around Puget Sound, sow directly in the ground from February into May, planting a new short row every few weeks for a steady harvest from late spring into midsummer; there's no need to start seed indoors. Right on the coast, OSU's own numbers are even more generous, spring sowing from January into spring and a second round in summer for a real fall crop, since the marine-cooled coastal summer never gets too hot for peas.
seasoned: Snow peas are direct sown here, not started indoors, per OSU's Oregon planting table. In the Willamette Valley that table gives a single continuous window, February through May, wide enough for repeated succession sowings but with no distinct fall window OSU extends to this region. The immediate coast tells a different story: OSU's own table runs January clear through August with no stated gap, an unusually long window this cell reads as a spring wave and a genuine second, summer-sown wave rather than one invented fall planting, since the crop's own maturity time naturally opens a short shoulder between them. Neither zone needs a summer heat exclusion; the region's mild, marine-tempered summer is exactly what this cool-season crop wants.

beginner: Snow peas are a spring-only crop in the Piedmont and Coastal Plain: sow directly in the ground very early, weeks before your last frost, since young pea plants shrug off cold. Pick through late spring into early summer, and then the vines stop as the real heat arrives. Virginia Cooperative Extension does not document a fall pea planting here, so there is no second sowing to plan for; enjoy the spring flush and move on to a warm-season crop for the rest of the year.
seasoned: Snow peas run a single, well-documented early-spring cycle here: Virginia Cooperative Extension's garden pea table opens in late February in zone 8 and early March in zone 7, weeks ahead of the last frost, since pea seedlings tolerate cold well. Vines crop through late spring into early summer and then decline once sustained heat sets in; VCE lists no fall sowing for garden peas in this belt, so the rest of the season is honestly left open rather than filled with an invented second cycle. (Virginia Cooperative Extension Pub. 426-331)

beginner: In the Las Vegas Valley, direct-sow snow peas outdoors in late winter, from about Feb 14 through Mar 16, for pods before the heat arrives. Once daytime highs push past 90°F, the vines stop setting pods, so pull them and let the bed rest. Sow again from about Sep 1 to Oct 5 for a fall crop that ripens as the weather cools, picked up to the first frost.
seasoned: The Las Vegas Valley grows snow peas on two direct-sown cycles, per the UNLV/UNR Cooperative Extension Master Gardener planting chart, which shades peas in February and March and again in September into October. Spring sowing runs roughly Feb 14 to Mar 16, with pods beginning about 62 days later; the vines are pulled before summer's real heat wall, since UNR Fact Sheet FS-02-61 puts the region's growth ceiling at about 90°F and peas fail to set pods well before that point is reached. The chart's fall window, about Sep 1 to Oct 5, restarts the crop as the heat breaks, cropping into cooler weather and picked up to the valley's first frost, which a light touch sweetens but a hard freeze ends. Zone 8's cooler pockets run both windows later than zone 9; zone 10 at Laughlin runs them earlier, with a later first frost stretching the fall harvest a little further.

beginner: Direct-sow snow peas in mid-February, about Feb 15, once the ground can be worked. Pods are ready to pick from mid-April into early May. There is no fall planting for peas here, so once the vines are pulled ahead of the summer heat, the bed rests until next spring.
seasoned: St. George grows snow peas on a single spring, direct-sown cycle, per USU Extension's "Suggested Vegetable Planting Dates for Utah," which sets Feb 15 as the St. George Group A (hardy) date for peas. Pods begin about 62 days later, and the vines are pulled by early May, well ahead of the 100°F heat St. George reaches from June into September. USU's planting-date table documents no fall pea window for the St. George area, unlike the handful of Group E crops (beets, cabbage, kale, lettuce, onion, spinach, turnip) that do get one, so this cell runs a single spring cycle rather than a fabricated second one.

beginner: Snow peas are the flat, tender peas you eat pod and all, stir-fried or raw, picked while the pods are still flat and the peas inside are tiny. They are a cool-weather crop: you plant the seeds straight in the garden as soon as the soil can be worked in spring, and again in late summer for fall, not in the heat of summer. Young plants handle frost, but the vines fade once it gets hot. Tall kinds need a trellis to climb; short kinds hold each other up. They go from seed to harvest in about two months and, like all peas, feed the soil with nitrogen. They are a close cousin of the plumper sugar snap pea.
seasoned: Snow peas (Pisum sativum) are a cool-season, frost-hardy legume grown for their flat, edible immature pods, picked young before the seeds swell (the mangetout type). Unlike warm-season beans, peas are sown as early as the soil can be worked in spring and again in fall, and they decline once summer heat passes about 80°F, so the season runs opposite a bean's. Climbing types need a trellis while bush types stand together; as a legume the crop fixes much of its own nitrogen and asks little feeding, reaching a flat, sweet pod in about 55 to 70 days. They are distinct from the sugar-snap pea, a cousin grown for plump, rounded pods eaten whole when filled.

beginner: Snow peas are ready when the pods are flat, bright green, and tender, before you can see the peas swelling inside, about a week after the flowers open. Pick every few days to keep more pods coming.
seasoned: Pick snow peas while the pods are flat, bright, and tender, before the seeds inside begin to swell, about a week after flowering. Harvesting every couple of days keeps the vines producing and catches the pods at peak sweetness.
